# On the Peculiar Joy of Noticing Things

I've been thinking lately about how much happiness comes from simply paying attention. Not the forced, grim attention of someone checking boxes, but the wandering kind—when you actually *see* something.

Like yesterday, I watched a pigeon navigate a crowded sidewalk by tilting its head side to side, its iridescent neck catching light in ways that seemed almost irresponsible for a bird most people dismiss instantly. For maybe thirty seconds, that pigeon was the most interesting thing in the world.

There's something radical about it, actually. We're all drowning in stimulation, yet somehow suffering from profound inattention. We scroll past thousands of images but remember none of them. Meanwhile, someone noticing the exact sound their shoes make on wet pavement, or the way afternoon light turns a stairwell golden, or how their friend's laugh has changed slightly since last year—those people seem to be living in a richer world.

I think this is what people mean when they talk about mindfulness, though that word has been marketing-branded into uselessness. They mean the opposite of absent-mindedness. They mean waking up to where you already are.

The funny part? It doesn't cost anything. You can't buy it. It just requires the radical act of stopping for a second. Of letting something ordinary become interesting because you're actually *looking* at it.

Maybe that's the real luxury—not more things, but deeper attention to the things already surrounding us. A life where pigeons matter. Where staircases glow. Where everything is interesting if you bother to notice.
